background.definition: Aortic valve stenosis (AS) is defined as an obstruction of the flow of blood from the left ventricle to the aorta as a consequence of aortic valve pathology. It is typically caused by premature calcification of a congenital bicuspid valve, age-related degenerative calcification of a normal trileaflet valve, or by rheumatic disease.

list.listitem: Calcific aortic valve stenosis is the most common valve disease in developed countries. Initial symptoms usually occur in the late 60s.

A bicuspid aortic valve is a major cause of AS in adults. Between 1% and 2% or the population is born with a bicuspid aortic valve. AS occurs in up to 72% of adults with a congenital bicuspid aortic valve, with a peak incidence in the 5th and 6th decade.
The prevalence of AS increases with age, occuring most commonly in persons older than 60 years. AS occurs in 2% of those older than 65 years and in 4% in those older than 85 years.
Critical AS was found in 2.9% of 75 to 86 year olds participating in the Helsinki aging study.
Age-related calcification of a bicuspid or normal, trileaflet, aortic valve is the most common cause of AS in older adults.
Calcification of congenitally bicuspid aortic valves leads to aortic stenosis.
Bicuspid valves are present in two-thirds of those undergoing AVR at an age younger than 70 and 40% of those older than 70.
Rheumatic fusion of the aortic valve commissures with subsequent scarring and calcification.
Valve obstruction in AS occurs over decades and leads to chronic left ventricular (LV) systolic and diastolic pressure overload.

LV systolic pressure overload leads to left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), which normalizes wall stress maintaining LV output for some time. Both LVH and an increase in LV diastolic pressure lead to increased myocardial oxygen consumption.

Decreased aortic pressure at the later stages of AS leads to a decrease in myocardial oxygen supply. Myocardial ischemia eventually results from the imbalance between the elevated myocardial oxygen consumption and the decreased myocardial oxygen supply, and can lead to chest pain with exertion.
As AS becomes more severe, the hypertrophied left ventricle can no longer maintain normal LV systolic wall stress and the elevated afterload leads to a decrease in ejection fraction (EF).

Clinical distinction between low EF secondary to decreased contractility or excess afterload is difficult but essential, since surgical correction is less beneficial when decreased contractility is present. A dobutamine stress echo can help to distinguish between the two conditions.
Suspect AS in patients with a systolic murmur radiating to the neck or clavicles, or symptoms such as exertional dyspnea, angina, or syncope/pre-syncope.C
If clinically suspected, order an echocardiogram. C
Exercise testing may be considered in asymptomatic patients with severe AS to elicit exercise-induced symptoms or abnormal blood pressure response. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Chest pain due to CAD is confirmed by a stress test or by coronary angiography, with normal echocardiogram
Syncope due to a stroke or carotid artery disease can be confirmed by carotid Doppler studies and CNS imaging
CHF from volume overload can be confirmed by physical examination and echocardiography

list.listitem: Mild AS: aortic jet velocity <3.0 m/s, mean gradient <20 mm Hg, and valve area >1.5 cm2
Moderate AS: aortic jet velocity 3.0 to 4.0 m/s, mean gradient 20 to 40 mm Hg, and valve area 1.0 to 1.5 cm2
Severe AS: aortic jet velocity >4.0 m/s, mean gradient >40 mm Hg, and valve area <1.0 cm2
A sub-category includes patients with low-flow, low-gradient severe AS (because of reduced LV systolic function)
Very severe AS: aortic jet velocity >5 m/s, mean gradient ≥60 mm Hg

Classic presenting symptoms are dyspnea on exertion, angina, and effort syncope, as well as pre-syncope and congestive heart failure symptoms. Patients classically have a harsh holosystolic ejection murmur heard best at the right upper sternal border and radiating up to the carotid arteries. The murmur time to peak correlates with severity of stenosis. Late systolic peaking indicates more severe stenosis.

Studies of diagnostic accuracy found the largest increase in the likelihood of aortic stenosis among patients with radiation to the clavicles and neck bilaterally (LR+ 12.4), followed by humming quality of murmur (LR+ 8.5) and radiation to right clavicle, right neck, or both (LR+ 2.4). Absence of radiation to the neck reduces the likelihood that a systolic murmur is caused by AS (LR− 0.2).
Pulsus parvus et tardus is a late-peaking and delayed carotid upstroke, and indicates severe AS. Normal carotid upstroke does not exclude severe AS. Another sign of AS is a sustained apical impulse.

A single second heart sound (S2) indicates that the aortic valve leaflets are immobile and no longer produce a second component of S2. Normal splitting of S2 rules out severe AS. AS murmur is augmented by squatting because of increased stroke volume going across the valve. Standing and the Valsalva maneuver reduce the AS murmur intensity.
Clinical diagnosis of heart failure by a cardiologist is highly accurate.

Echocardiography is the standard for evaluation of patients with AS murmur. An echocardiogram should be performed on asymptomatic patients with the following murmur types: diastolic, continuous holosystolic, late systolic, radiating to the neck or back and murmurs with ejection clicks. It is also useful for assessing the degree of heart failure in patients with aortic stenosis, as is b-natriuretic peptide (BNP). N-terminal BNP >1200 pmol/L increases the likelihood of heart failure in patients with AS, as does pulmonary capillary web pressure greater than 12 mm Hg (LR+ 7.1) or 14 mm Hg (LR+ 16.0).

An echocardiogram is not needed in patients with a grade 1 or 2 midsystolic murmur felt to be innocent or functional (e.g., no other abnormal sounds, systolic ejection pattern, normal intensity and splitting of S2, no evidence of LVH).
ECG shows evidence of LVH in 85% and left atrial enlargement in 80% of patients with severe AS. CXR may show signs of left ventricular or left atrial enlargement as well.
Exercise testing should be avoided in symptomatic patients, due to the risk of serious complications, but may be useful for guiding therapy in patients with AS who are asymptomatic.

Cardiac catheterization is recommended before aortic valve replacement surgery in patients who are at risk for coronary artery disease: cardiac catheterization is not needed to assess the severity of AS, when clinical symptoms and non-invasive studies are consistent and adequate.
Chest CT may be useful to evaluate aortic root dilitation extent.

Clinical decision rules have been developed and validated to predict the need for AV replacement, in patients with aortic stenosis and to predict the need for permanent pacing after cardiac valve surgery.
Suspect AS in patients with systolic murmur radiating to the neck or clavicles. Manifestations of severe AS are exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope, and heart failure.
When AS or other valvular heart disease is clinically suspected, order ECG, CXR, and a cardiac echocardiogram that measures transaortic flow velocity.

Treadmill exercise testing can be helpful in evaluating asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis to determine their levels of symptoms, hemodynamic response to exercise, or prognosis; care should be taken when performing treadmill exercise testing on patients with known severe aortic stenosis our of concern for hypotension.

Flow velocities <3 m/s are associated with a 3% risk of symptoms within the subsequent 5 years. Annual re-evaluation with history, physical and echo study is reasonable for this group. Flow velocities >4 m/s are associated with a 70% chance that valve replacement will be required within 2 years.

For patients with severe AS (gradient >40 mm Hg, jet velocity >4 m/s, area <1.0 cm2) who are symptomatic should be referred for SAVR or TAVR. In those with equivocal symptoms, order an exercise test, and if symptomatic, refer for AVR. For patients who are not symptomatic, evaluate the LV ejection fraction. If <50%, or if rapid progression expected, refer for AVR. Otherwise, unless patient has another indication for surgery such as CABG, follow-up with clinical evaluation, and echocardiography annually.
The risk of sudden death in patients with severe aortic stenosis is 1% per year.
Guidelines recommend that patients with severe aortic stenosis be evaluated and managed by a team that is at least comprised of a cardiologist and a cardiac surgeon.
Patients with bicuspid aortic valve should undergo at least one imaging test to assess their aortic root for dilatation. Screening of first degree family members should be performed.

Some patients manifest aortic stenosis pathophysiology, although measured gradients are below the "severe" threshold, such as "low gradient aortic stenosis" (in the setting of cardiomyopathy). A dobutamine stress echo can help to identify if the low calculated valve area is a result of true valve stenosis versus inadequate valve opening from a weakened left ventricle.
Patients with symptomatic severe aortic valve stenosis and selected patients with asymptomatic severe AS should undergo valve replacement.B
Patients with asymptomatic moderate aortic valve stenosis should undergo valve replacement if they need to undergo CABG.B
Aortic balloon valvuloplasty is reasonable as a bridge to aortic valve replacement in high-risk patients or as palliation in non-surgery candidates.C
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is a percutaneous approach to severe aortic stenosis. It is recommended for appropriate patients with moderate to high surgical risk.A

After transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), patients are generally given an anti-platelet agent unless they also have an indication for anti-coagulation. A meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials with 4805 patients found that when compared with dual anti-platelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel, patients given aspirin alone had fewer all-cause bleeding (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.29-0.57), less major bleeding (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.77), and were less likely to require a transfusion (OR 0.39, 95% CI 0.15-0.98). There was no difference between groups in the likelihood of mortality, stroke rate, prosthetic valve thrombosis, TIA, or cardiovascular mortality.

The combination of rivaroxaban and aspirin following TAVR is not recommended. An RCT with 1644 patients found an increased risk of death, thromboembolic complications, and bleeding than in a group receiving 3 months of dual anti-platelet therapy followed by aspirin.

A randomized trial with 620 patients with aortic stenosis, heart failure who were undergoing TAVR found that dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily significantly reduced the likelihood of worsening heart failure (9.4% vs 14.4%) and slightly (but not significantly) reduced mortality (7.8% vs 8.9%, p=NS).

Management with drug therapy should be reserved for patients who are not surgical candidates. Medical therapy does not delay progression or reduce mortality. Options include cautious use of diuretics, digitalis, and ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers. Nitroprusside infusion can be given in the ICU to treat acute heart failure symptoms.
Statins do not impact the incidence of aortic valve stenosis. Likewise statins have not been shown to slow progression or induce regression of AS in patients with calcific aortic stenosis.

Aortic valve replacement should be considered as an effective way to improve health-related quality of life in elderly patients who are appropriately referred for surgery. Aortic valve replacement is recommended by 2020 ACC guidelines for the following groups:
Adults with severe high-gradient AS and who are symptomatic Asymptomatic adults with severe AS who have a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) < 50% Asymptomatic adults with severe AS undergoing cardiac surgery for another reason. Symptomatic adults with low-flow, low-gradient severe AS and a reduced LVEF; it should be considered in those with normal LVEF if it is thought to the most likely reason for symptoms. Asymptomatic patients with severe AS, low surgical risk, and decreased exercise tolerance or asymptomatic adults with very severe AS (aortic velocity >= 5 m/s) and low surgical risk. Consider AVR for asymptomatic patients with severe AS, low surgical risk, and BNP > 3 times upper limit of normal Consider AVR for asymptomatic patients with high-gradient severe AS and low surgical risk when serial testing shows aortic velocity increasing by >= 0.3 m/s/year. Consider AVR for patients with moderate AS having cardiac surgery for another indication.

The US and European guidelines for management of severe AS differ with regards to the LVEF at which to intervene (55% for European vs 60% after serial imaging for US), and with regards to age cutoffs for surgery.

The AVATAR trial identified 157 patients with asymptomatic severe AS, normal exercise test, and normal LVEF. They were randomized to early surgical AVR or conservative therapy. The primary composite endpoint of death, MI, stroke, or heart failure hospitalizaiton was less likely in the early surgery group (15.2% vs 34.7%, HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.23-0.90, NNT = 5). While individual endpoints were not significantly lower, all cause mortality was numerically lower in the early surgery group (9% vs 20%). A 5 year follow-up found persistent benefit, with the composite outcome occurring less in the early surgery groupo (23.1% vs 46.8%, p<.001, NNT = 4).

An RCT identified 145 patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis, defined as aortic valve area <= 0.75 cm2 and either aortic jet velocity >= 4.5 m/sec or mean transaortic gradient >= 50 mm Hg. They were randomized to early surgery within 2 months or to conservative care; in the latter group 74% ultimately underwent aortic valve replacement a median of 2 years later. The primary outcome of operative mortality or cardiovascular death occurred significantly less often in the early surgery group (1% vs 15%, HR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01-0.67, NNT = 7).

A study randomized 455 patients to with severe, asymptomatic AS to early TAVR or clinical surveillance. The composite of death, stroke, or unplanned hospital admission was less common with early TAVR (26.8% vs 45.3%) but was driven primarily by fewer hospitalizations. After 4 years over 80% in the surveillance group had undergone TAVR.
In a large prospective cohort study, patients receiving a biologic aortic valve prosthesis had higher 15 year mortality than those receiving a mechanical prosthesis (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.02-1.48).

A trial randomized patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) to continued anticoagulation or interruption of anticoagulation periprocedurally. The continuation group had a numerically higher incidence of major bleeding events and major vascular complications but no differences in thromboembolic events compared with the interrupted group.

In patients with stable but significant CAD who undergo TAVI, a randomized trial with 255 patients found that routine PCI leads to fewer major adverse cardiac events at a follow-up of 2 years. On average, for every 10 such patients, PCI would result in one less event.
Aortic balloon valvuloplasty is an option when patients are not candidates for surgery (i.e., palliation) or as a bridge to valve replacement for patients who are hemodynamically unstable.

TAVR is a percutaneous approach to severe aortic stenosis. It is recommended for appropriate patients with moderate to high surgical risk from AVR. In subjects at high risk for surgical complications, TAVR has similar rates of survival but at the expense of higher stroke risk and vascular complications. The PARTNER2 and PARTNER3 trials discussed below show that it is increasingly a good option for patients at low surgical risk as well.

The 2014 guidelines from the American College of Cardiology recommend TAV for patients who meet an indication for AVR for AS but who have a prohibitive surgical risk and predicted post-operative survival of at least 12 months. It is a reasonable options for those at high surgical risk as well. It is not recommended when comorbidities make the patient unlikely to benefit. Updated 2017 guidelines add TAVR as an option for patients at intermediate surgical risk.

Recent meta-analyses have demonstrated similar cardiovascular and all-cause mortality for TAVR versus surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) at early and long-term follow up, with lower bleeding complications.

A study identified 1414 low-risk patients with severe, symptomatic AS who were candidates for both TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). Death or stroke at one year occurred less often in the TAVR group (5.4% v 10.0%, HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.35-0.79, NNT = 22).
In subjects with intermediate risk of perioperative complications, TAVR was associated with similar outcomes with regard to death or disabling stroke.

Another RCT randomized 1746 intermediate surgical risk patients with AS to TAVR or surgical replacement (mean age 80 years). TAVR was non-inferior for the combined outcome of death or disabling stroke at 24 months (12.6% for TAVR vs 14.0% for surgery). Patients in the TAVR group were more likely to have residual regurgitation and were more likely to need a pacemaker, while those in the surgery group were more likely to have acute kidney injury and atrial fibrillation.

The PARTNER2 trial randomized 2032 patients to TAVR or surgical valve replacement (mean age 81, 5.8% predicted operative mortality). There was no significant difference between the 2 groups for the composite outcome of all-cause death or disabling stroke at 5 years (48% in TAVR group vs 43% in surgery group; P = 0.21). The TAVR group was more likely to be re-hospitalized (33.3% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio [HR] 1.28; 95% CI 1.07-1.53) and require re-intervention of the aortic valve (3.2% vs 0.8%; HR 3.28; 1.32-8.13), but less likely to have new-onset atrial fibrillation (15.8% vs 30.4%; HR 0.43; 0.35-0.53).

The PARTNER3 trial randomized 1000 low-risk surgical patients with symptomatic severe AS to TAVR or surgery. After 7 years of follow-up, there was no significant difference between groups with regards to the primary composite of death, stroke or rehospitalization and no difference for any of the individual components. However, stroke (1.2% vs 3.3%, hazard ratio [HR] 0.36, 95% CI 0.14–0.92) and rehospitalization (7.3% vs 11.5%, HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.95) were significantly less likely in the first year after the procedure in the TAVR group. Among secondary outcomes, left bundle branch block (21.1% vs 9.9%, HR 2.25, 95% CI 1.58-3.20) and clinically significant valve thrombosis (2.8% vs 0.5%, HR 5.70, 95% CI 1.29-25.3) were significantly more common with TAVR after 7 years. For the composite of death or disabling stroke, the early advantage of TAVR (1.0% vs 3.1%, HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.11-0.89) is reversed after the first year (20.9% vs 14.1%, HR 1.56, 95% CI 1.12-2.18). Similar results were seen in an RCT with 370 low risk younger patients with AS randomized to TAVR or surgery.
Among inoperable patients with severe AS, TAVR reduced the risk of cardiovascular death.

Patients with concomitant moderate-severe mitral regurgitation have increased mortality following TAVR relative to counterparts without severe valve disease. Half of patients show improvement in mitral regurgitation severity after TAVR.

A trial of 716 patients with severe AS and a small aortic annulus who were undergoing TAVR randomized them to a balloon-expandable valve or a self-expanding supra-annular valve. At 12 months for the composite of death, disabling stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure the self-expanding valve was non-inferior to the balloon-expandable valve.
A systematic review and meta analysis of 2408 patients over 39 studies described 66% had silent brain infarcts by MRI, but only 3% reported clinical stroke findings.

In an RCT of 455 patients with stable but significant CAD who underwent TAVI, routine PCI leads to fewer major adverse cardiac events at a follow-up of 2 years compared to no PCI. On average, for every 10 such patients, PCI would result in one less event.
Patients with moderate to severe stenosis who are asymptomatic have a good prognosis. Sudden death prior to development of symptoms occurs in about 1%/year. B
Once a patient develops symptoms, the mean survival is less than 3 years.B

In patients with moderate AS, the natural history is for an increase in the pressure gradient of 7 mm Hg/year and 0.3 m/s per year for jet velocity. Patients with jet velocity <3 m/s have 84% event free survival at 2 years, while those with jet velocity >4 m/s have an event free survival of 21% at 2 years.B

Patients with no symptoms with exercise have an 89% event free survival at 1 year, while those with symptoms during exercise have only a 49% event free survival at 1 year. Patients with symptomatic severe AS with LV failure and low cardiac output have the poorest prognosis. B

Once aortic stenosis is diagnosed, transthoracic echo should be performed in asymptomatic patients at the following intervals: yearly for severe AS, every 1 to 2 years for moderate AS, every 3 to 5 years for mild AS.B
Evaluation of surgical or interventional risk can be performed by using the predicted risk of mortality (PROM) calculator from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS).
Be aware of the need to have aortic valve replacement once symptoms start to occur.
Keep a log of your physical activity to make it easier to recognize the onset of shortness of breath with exertion.
